L79: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed mechanism and strategy design in mitigating entropy collapse, achieving more precise entropy control and markedly enhancing model performance for RLVR.
L80: ## 2 Preliminary
L81: ### 2.1 RL Algorithms of LLMs
L82: The PPO-Clip (cite56†Schulman et al., 2017 ) algorithm addresses the difficulty of determining the appropriate step size in Vanilla Policy Gradient (cite59†Williams, 1992 ) methods by clipping the policy update ratio, effectively approximating the trust region constraint of Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) (cite60†Schulman et al., 2015a ). Specifically, PPO employs an Actor-Critic architecture (cite61†Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ).
L83: Its core mechanism relies on limiting the divergence between the new and old policies via clipping, thereby preventing drastic policy drift during single updates.
L84: The importance sampling ratio $r_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})}{\pi_{old}(a_{t}|s_{t})}$ is defined as the ratio between the new policy $\pi_{\theta}$ and the old policy $\pi_{old}$. The objective function of PPO-Clip, denoted as $L^{C}$, seeks to maximize the advantage function $A_{t}$ while imposing a constraint on $r_{t}(\theta)$:
L85:  | $$L^{C}(\theta)=\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{t}\left[\min\left(r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{t},\text{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{t}\right)\right]\textrm{ .}$$  |
L86: 
L87: To more conveniently characterize the clipping threshold in PPO-Clip, we adopt a visualization method similar to that in (cite58†Wang et al., 2025a ), as shown in cite62†Figure 2(a) . Different colors represent different sizes of the clipping threshold. Generally, we choose $\epsilon_{low}=\epsilon_{high}=0.2$ (cite56†Schulman et al., 2017 ).
L88: In PPO-Clip, $\hat{A}_{t}$ is typically computed using Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (cite63†Schulman et al., 2015b ), which relies on an independent value network (Critic) to estimate state values. To enhance training efficiency and stability, GRPO (cite45†Shao et al., 2024 ) employs a group-based advantage estimation method that dispenses with the separate Critic.
L89: For a given question $q$, a set of outputs $\{o_{1},o_{2},...,o_{G}\}$ is sampled, yielding corresponding rewards $\{r_{1},r_{2},...,r_{G}\}$. GRPO calculates the advantage $A_{i}$ for the $i$-th output as its standardized score relative to the group mean:
L90:  | $$A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(\{r_{1},...,r_{G}\})}{\text{std}(\{r_{1},...,r_{G}\})+\delta}\textrm{ .}$$  |

L98: ### 2.2 The Policy Entropy of LLMs
L99: 
L100: The policy entropy of the model characterizes the degree of uncertainty at the current decision point, or equivalently, the ‘flatness’ of the model’s policy. Let $V$ denote the vocabulary space. At time step $t$, given the context $s_{t}$, the policy entropy $H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s_{t}))$ is defined as:
L101: 
L102:  | $$H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s_{t}))=-\sum_{a\in V}\pi_{\theta}(a|s_{t})\log\pi_{\theta}(a|s_{t})\textrm{ .}$$  |
L103: The work (cite51†Cui et al., 2025 ) reveals a predictable relationship between policy entropy and performance. Specifically, there exists a negative exponential correlation between the model’s policy entropy $H$ and model performance $R$:
L104: 
L105:  | $$R=a\times exp(H)+b\textrm{ .}$$  |
L106: 
L107: This equation indicates that the policy performance is achieved at the expense of the policy entropy, and when the entropy is exhausted, the performance reaches its upper limit.
L108: Through theoretical analysis, the work (cite52†Shen, 2025 ) demonstrates that entropy collapse severely impairs the model’s output diversity. Consequently, this restricts the update gradients during continual training, leading to a degradation in the model’s final performance. This is also reflected in cite55†Figure 1 .
L109: 
L110: Specifically, in RL training without entropy control, the norm of the final policy gradient is limited by the policy entropy:
L111:  | $$\|\nabla V^{\pi_{\theta}}(\mathcal{D})\|\leq 2H(\pi_{\theta})\textrm{ .}$$  |
L112: ## 3 Theoretical and Empirical Investigations
L113: To address Research Question 1: “How can we devise the regulation mechanism to precisely control the ebb and flow of entropy”, we conduct theoretical analyzes regarding the angle between RL training gradients and model entropy gradients. The theoretical analysis identifies the precise representation of four distinct importance sampling ratio regions on entropy dynamics during training. For empirical investigation, similar to those in cite65†Su et al. (2025) and cite66†Hao et al.
L114: (2025) , we verify the impacts of these four regions on policy entropy.
L115: We first provide the theoretical analysis. For a specific token $a$, we define the surrogate objective function for a single-step update as:
L116: 
L117:  | $$L(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a|s)}\hat{A}\textrm{ ,}$$  |  | (1)
L118: where $\pi_{\theta}(a|s)$ denotes the probability of the token under the current policy, $\pi_{\text{old}}(a|s)$ represents the probability under the sampling policy, and $\hat{A}$ is the advantage function. Assuming the policy $\pi_{\theta}$ is parameterized by logits $z$ (where $\pi(x)=\text{Softmax}(z)_{x}$), the gradient of the objective function $L$ for a specific token $a$ with respect to the logits $z$ is:
L119:  | $$\nabla_{z}L\propto\hat{A}\cdot\nabla_{z}\ln\pi_{\theta}(a|s)=\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})\textrm{ ,}$$  |  | (2)
L120: 
L121: where $\mathbf{e}_{a}$ is the one-hot vector for token $a$, and $\mathbf{p}$ is the probability vector over the entire vocabulary.
L122: 
L123: Next, we consider the global entropy:
L124: 
L125:  | $$H(\pi)=-\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}\ln p_{x}\textrm{ .}$$  |  | (3)
L126: 
L127: The gradient of $H$ with respect to the logits $z$ is derived as:
L128:  | $$\nabla_{z}H=-\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})\textrm{ ,}$$  |  | (4)
L129: 
L130: where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication and $\mathbf{1}$ is a vector of ones. To determine whether the reinforcement learning update increases or decreases entropy, we compute the inner product between the objective gradient $\nabla_{z}L$ and the global entropy gradient $\nabla_{z}H$:
L131:  | $\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{z}L,$  | $\displaystyle\nabla_{z}H\rangle\propto\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})^{\top}\left[-\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})\right]$  |
L132:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\hat{A}\left[\underbrace{p_{a}(\ln p_{a}+H)}_{\text{Token-specific term}}-\underbrace{\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}^{2}(\ln p_{x}+H)}_{\text{Global baseline term}}\right]\textrm{ .}$  |  | (5)
L133: For a more detailed derivation of cite67†Section B.1 , please refer to cite27†Section B.1 . The second term represents an expectation over the vocabulary (weighted by squared probabilities). Since we are analyzing the gradient contribution of a specific token update, the sign is primarily determined by the token-specific term relative to the baseline. Focusing on the token-specific component, we obtain the following relationship:
L134:  | $$\operatorname{sgn}(\langle\nabla_{\theta}L,\nabla_{\theta}H\rangle)\approx-\operatorname{sgn}\left(\hat{A}\cdot[\ln\pi_{\theta}(a|s)+H]\right)\textrm{ .}$$  |  | (6)
L135: 
L136: This derivation suggests that the change in entropy depends on the Surprisal of token $a$ ($-\ln\pi(a|s)$) relative to the current Entropy ($H$) of the distribution.
L137: 
L138: Assuming positive advantage ($\hat{A}>0$):
L139: 
L140:   * •
L141: Entropy Decreases (E1) if $-\ln\pi(a|s)<H$ : If the token $a$ is less surprising than average (high probability), encouraging it further sharpens the distribution.
L142: 
L143:   * •
L144: 
L145: Entropy Increases (E2) if $-\ln\pi(a|s)>H$ : If the token $a$ is more surprising than average (low probability), encouraging it flattens the distribution.
L146: 
L147: Assuming negative advantage ($\hat{A}<0$):
L148: 
L149:   * •
L150: Entropy Increases (E3) if $-\ln\pi(a|s)<H$ : If the token $a$ is less surprising than average (high probability), discouraging it flattens the distribution.
L151: 
L152:   * •
L153: 
L154: Entropy Decreases (E4) if $-\ln\pi(a|s)>H$ : If the token $a$ is more surprising than average (low probability), discouraging it further sharpens the distribution.
L155: To validate our theoretical findings, we test the four regions (E1–E4) within the extended PPO-Clip trust region ($0.7<r<1.3$) characterized by high ($\pi_{\theta}>0.7$) or low ($\pi_{\theta}<0.3$) probability (Figure cite68†2(b) ). We applied Gradient-Preserving Clipping exclusively to these regions, while ensuring theoretically unaffected tokens (e.g., $\pi_{\text{old}}>\pi_{\theta}$ given $A>0$) continued training normally. Results are shown in Figure cite69†2(c) .
L156: ## 4 Methodology
L157: 
L158: Based on the above understanding of the impact of each region in PPO-Clip on entropy in cite10†Section 3 . cite12†Section 4.1 builds upon these findings to propose a regulation mechanism capable of stably controlling entropy fluctuations. To address Research Question 2: “Grounded on this mechanism, how can we design the entropy control strategy for effective RL training?”, we present three training strategies in cite15†Section 4.2 based on rational entropy evolution.
L159: ### 4.1 Regulation Mechanism for Entropy Variations
L160: 
L161: We will separately design and discuss a dynamic upper clipping threshold to regulate the increase entropy, and a dynamic lower clipping threshold to control the decrease entropy.
L162: 
L163: (a)
L164:

L168: #### 4.1.1 Dynamic Upper Clipping Threshold
L169: 
L170: The upper clipping threshold mainly performs gradient clipping on tokens where the current policy probability is already somewhat higher than the rollout policy probability when $A>0$. DAPO (cite54†Yu et al., 2025 ) believes that the upper clipping threshold in RL limits the probability increase of low-probability tokens in positive samples (E2).
L171: However, the fixed adoption of a higher clipping threshold, in addition to introducing low-probability tokens (E2) into training, also introduces high-probability tokens (E1) into the computation. Since the current policy probability of these tokens is already somewhat higher than the rollout policy probability, if they continue to participate in gradient computation, it will inevitably reduce the diversity of the model’s output.
L172: When $A>0$, we propose adjusting the upper clipping threshold of PPO-Clip: increasing it for low-probability tokens to facilitate their growth, while decreasing it for high-probability tokens to prevent over-optimization and preserve exploration.
L173: 
L174: Specifically, We reformulate the clipping threshold $\epsilon$ not as a constant, but as a dynamic function of the current probability, denoted as $\epsilon(\pi_{\theta})$:
L175: 
L176:  | $$\epsilon(\pi_{\theta}):=f(\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t}))\textrm{ .}$$  |  | (7)
L177: Among them, $f(\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t}))$ should be a function that is negatively correlated with $\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})$. To ensure the numerical stability of the function and the reliability of the analysis results, we consider the case where this function has a linear negative correlation $\epsilon(\pi_{\theta})=\alpha\cdot\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})+\beta$.
L178: Therefore, a non-linear dynamic upper clipping threshold can be obtained, and the relationship between $\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})$ and $\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_{t}|s_{t})$ is as follows:
L179: 
L180:  | $$\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\leq\frac{1+\beta}{1-\alpha\cdot\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_{t}|s_{t})}\cdot\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_{t}|s_{t})\textrm{ .}$$  |  | (8)
L181: Relative to the DAPO baseline, we calibrated the upper clipping threshold to exceed $\epsilon_{high}$ in the low-probability regime while remaining lower in the high-probability regime (cite70†Figure 3(a) ). In the context of cite10†Section 3 , this adjusts thresholds in the E1 and E2 regions to intentionally increase model entropy. As expected, cite71†Figure 6(a) show a steady rise in entropy and a corresponding decline in performance.
L182: #### 4.1.2 Dynamic Lower Clipping Threshold
L183: The lower clipping threshold mainly performs gradient clipping on tokens where the current policy probability is already somewhat lower than the rollout policy probability when $A<0$. Unlike when $A>0$, when $A<0$, there is an instability caused by negative signals (cite72†Gao et al., 2025 ). Let $z$ denote the logits (defined over vocabulary $V$), let $x$ denote a generic token, and compute output probabilities via a softmax operation.
L184: Considering the gradient of the objective for a specific sampled token $a$ with respect to the logit of a generic token $x$ (denoted as $z_{x}$):
L185:  | $$\begin{split}\frac{\partial(\ln\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\cdot\hat{A})}{\partial z_{x}}&=\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\partial z_{x}}\cdot\frac{\hat{A}}{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}\\
L186: &\hskip-50.0pt=\begin{cases}(1-\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s))\cdot\hat{A}&\text{if }x=a\\
L187: -\pi_{\theta}(x\mid s)\cdot\hat{A}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\textrm{ .}\end{split}$$  |  | (9)
L188: A more detailed analysis of cite73†Equation 10 can be found in cite28†Section B.2 . Since Softmax normalization forces all other token probabilities to rise when a sampled token is penalized, inaccurate tokens may be inadvertently boosted (cite72†Gao et al., 2025 ). A fixed high $\epsilon_{low}$ exacerbates this by allowing excessive updates to high-probability tokens, causing significant distribution shifts.
L189: Therefore, we dynamically reduce $\epsilon_{low}$ for high-probability negative samples to maintain stability.
L190: Conversely, regarding low-probability tokens, since their contribution to the overall distribution is minimal, further suppressing their probabilities via negative advantages exerts a relatively limited impact on the global policy. We argue for dynamically adjusting $\epsilon_{low}$ by moderately extending the $\epsilon_{low}$ for low-probability negative samples. Theoretically, this approach yields two beneficial effects:
L191: Balancing the “Exploration/Exploitation” trade-off in policy updates: Further compression of low-probability tokens with negative advantages reinforces the exclusion of sub-optimal regions and enhances policy concentration, without disrupting established optimal behaviors as penalizing high-probability tokens would.
L192: Mitigating “ineffective clipping” of gradients: Utilizing a larger $\epsilon_{low}$ allows these low-probability, negative-advantage tokens to receive more sufficient negative gradients within a reasonable range.
L193: 
L194: Similarly, we use the linear negative correlation method to adjust the lower clipping threshold, as shown in cite74†Figure 3(b) . This strategy decreases model entropy by extending the threshold in the E4 region and reducing it in E3. As expected, cite75†Figure 6(b) show a steady decrease in entropy.

L202: ### 4.2 Strategy Design for Entropy Control
L203: 
L204: As shown in cite9†Section 2.2 , RL training should follow a dynamic entropy strategy: maintaining high entropy in the early stages to promote flexible exploration, while gradually reducing it in later stages to achieve optimal performance and output stability. Excessive entropy causes instability, while premature reduction hinders exploration. Leveraging the adjustment mechanism from cite12†Section 4.1 , we further design entropy control strategies for LLMs.
L205: We generalize the PPO clipped objective function into a time-dependent formulation. At training step $k\in[0,T_{max}]$, the loss function is defined as:
L206: 
L207:  | $$\begin{split}L^{CLIP}_{k}(\theta)=\hat{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{t=1}^{G}\min\Big(r_{t}(\theta)A_{t},\text{clip}(r_{t}(\theta)&,\\
L208: 1-{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{E}^{-}_{k}(p_{t})},1+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{E}^{+}_{k}(p_{t})})A_{t}\Big)\Bigg]&\textrm{ .}\end{split}$$  |
L209: Here, the clipping threshold $\mathcal{E}_{k}$ is a function of the current policy probability $p_{t}$, with parameters that evolve over the global step $k$. This function regulates the scaling of the upper and lower bounds according to the current training stage. We explore three specific control strategies: (1) an increase-then-decrease (ID) mode; (2) a decrease-increase-decrease (DID) mode; and (3) an oscillatory decay (OD) mode within a limited entropy bound.
L210: To balance entropy maintenance with convergence precision, we propose two scheduling strategies, denoted as ID and DID, which utilize $T/2$ as the bifurcation point.
L211: 
L212: Increase-then-Decrease: We define a baseline threshold $\epsilon_{std}=0.2$ and a temporal scaling factor $\lambda(k)=1-\frac{2k}{T_{max}}$.
L213: 
L214:   * •
L215: Phase I ($k<T/2$): The lower clipping threshold is fixed at $\epsilon_{std}$. Simultaneously, we apply a linear decay to the dynamic upper clipping threshold $\mathcal{H}(p)$ (defined in cite13†Section 4.1.1 ), gradually annealing it toward $\epsilon_{std}$.
L216: 
L217:   * •
L218: Phase II ($k\geq T/2$): The upper clipping threshold remains constant at $\epsilon_{std}$. We then introduce a linear gain to progressively transform the lower clipping threshold from $\epsilon_{std}$ to the dynamic lower clipping threshold $\mathcal{M}(p)$ (defined in cite14†Section 4.1.2 ).
L219: 
L220: The schematic illustration of this scheduling process is presented in cite78†Figure 4 . The resulting training objective function is formulated as follows:
L221:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}$  | $\displaystyle{}^{+}_{k-ID}(p),\mathcal{E}^{-}_{k-ID}(p)=$  |
L222:  |  | $\displaystyle\begin{cases}\lambda_{k}\cdot\mathcal{H}(p)+(1-\lambda_{k})\cdot\epsilon_{std},\quad\epsilon_{std}&0\leq k\leq\frac{T}{2}\\
L223: \epsilon_{std},\quad(1+\lambda_{k})\cdot\mathcal{M}(p)-\lambda_{k}\cdot\epsilon_{std}&\frac{T}{2}<k\leq T\textrm{ .}\end{cases}$  |
L224: Decrease-Increase-Decrease: Unlike the ID, the DID control strategy allows the model entropy to first decrease in the first phase, controls the increase of model entropy through gradient clipping before entropy collapse, and then controls the model convergence in the second phase.
L225: 
L226:   * •
L227: Phase I ($k<T/2$): The lower clipping threshold is fixed at $\epsilon_{std}$. We then introduce a linear gain to progressively transition the upper clipping threshold from $\epsilon_{std}$ to the dynamic upper clipping threshold $\mathcal{H}(p)$
L228: 
L229:   * •
L230: Phase II ($k\geq T/2$): The upper clipping threshold remains constant at $\mathcal{H}(p)$. We then introduce a linear gain to progressively transition the lower clipping threshold from $\epsilon_{std}$ to the dynamic lower clipping threshold $\mathcal{M}(p)$.
L231: 
L232: The schematic illustration of this scheduling process is presented in cite79†Figure 5 . The resulting training objective function is formulated as follows:
L233:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}$  | $\displaystyle{}^{+}_{k-DID}(p),\mathcal{E}^{-}_{k-DID}(p)=$  |
L234:  |  | $\displaystyle\begin{cases}\lambda_{k}\cdot\epsilon_{std}+(1-\lambda_{k})\cdot\mathcal{H}(p),\quad\epsilon_{std}&0\leq k\leq\frac{T}{2}\\
L235: \mathcal{H}(p),\quad(1+\lambda_{k})\cdot\mathcal{M}(p)-\lambda_{k}\cdot\epsilon_{std}&\frac{T}{2}<k\leq T\textrm{ .}\end{cases}$  |
L236: Oscillatory Decay: Both ID and DID control strategies partition the training process into two distinct stages. In contrast, the OD control strategy is designed to enable the model to undergo autonomous oscillatory attenuation throughout the training duration. Specifically, we begin by defining a pair of entropy thresholds that evolve in relation to the training step $k$:
L237:  | $\displaystyle\tau_{low}$  | $\displaystyle=H_{min}\textrm{ ,}$  |
L238:  | $\displaystyle\tau_{high}(t)$  | $\displaystyle=H_{min}+(H_{init}-H_{min})\cdot(1-\frac{t}{T})\textrm{ ,}$  |
L239: where $H(\pi_{t})$ denotes the entropy of the current policy and $H_{min}$ represents the target entropy lower bound, which is defined here as $0.2H_{init}$. We introduce a discrete state variable $s_{k}\in\{0,1\}$ to characterize the current control mode (where $1$ signifies the entropy-increasing mode and $0$ signifies the entropy-decreasing mode). The state transitions are governed by hysteresis logic.
L240:  | $$s_{k}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }H(\pi_{t})\leq\tau_{low}\quad(\text{Trigger Boost})\\
L241: 0&\text{if }H(\pi_{t})>\tau_{high}(k)\quad(\text{Trigger Suppress})\textrm{ .}\\
L242: \end{cases}$$  |
L243: 
L244: Based on the current state $s_{k}$, the dynamic clipping threshold $\mathcal{E}^{+}_{k}(p)$ and $\mathcal{E}^{-}_{k}(p)$ are defined as follows:
L245:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{+}_{k}(p),\mathcal{E}^{-}_{k}(p)=$  | $\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathcal{H}(p),\quad\epsilon_{std}&\text{if }s_{k}=1\\
L246: \epsilon_{std},\quad\mathcal{M}(p)&\text{if }s_{k}=0\textrm{ .}\end{cases}$  |
L247: ## 5 Experiments
L248: 
L249: In this section, we report the experimental results on the effectiveness of entropy control and model performance across benchmarks, and provide the analysis of phase ratios. More experimental setup and results are given in Appendix.
L250: ### 5.1 Experimental Setup
L251: To validate our proposed training strategies, we train Qwen2.5-Math-7B (cite80†Yang et al., 2024 ) and Qwen2.5-7B (cite80†Yang et al., 2024 ) on the DAPO-MATH dataset. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of mathematical performance across the AIME24 (cite81†Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ), AIME25 (cite82†Zhang and Math-AI, 2025 ), , GSM8k (cite83†Cobbe et al., 2021 ), AMC, MATH-500, and Olympiad (cite84†Lightman et al., 2023 ) benchmarks.
L252: To ensure reliability, we averaged results across multiple runs: 32 for AIME24, AIME25, and AMC (Including AMC22, AMC23, AMC24); 4 for MATH-500 and Olympiad; and 2 for GSM8k. In addition to the original GRPO, we selected several baselines related to clipping threshold mechanisms, including Clip-Higher (cite54†Yu et al., 2025 ), Clip-Lower, Entropy-Regularization, Clip-Cov (cite51†Cui et al., 2025 ), GSPO(cite85†Zheng et al., 2025 ) and SAPO (cite72†Gao et al., 2025 ).
L253: Training configurations included a learning rate of $1\times 10^{-6}$, a sampling rate of 8 responses per prompt, and a global batch size of 512. The maximum response length was set to 4096 tokens for Qwen2.5-Math-7B and 8192 tokens for Qwen2.5-7B. Further training details are provided in the cite29†Appendix C . Further evaluation details are provided in the cite34†Appendix D .

L255: ### 5.2 Experimental Results and Analysis
L256: 
L257: The results of the training experiments on the dynamic upper clipping threshold and dynamic lower clipping threshold are shown in cite86†Figure 6 , which can prove that our control over entropy increase and entropy decrease is effective.
L258: The experimental results are shown in cite87†Table 1 . We can see that our three training strategies all demonstrate the performance of our method on multiple benchmarks. Building on this, we further analyze the entropy and performance cite19†Section 5.3 , and the setting of training phase ratios cite20†Section 5.4 in the training process of our method.
L259: The remaining results including the analysis of the average clipping threshold, the analysis of the clipping probability and the experiment on replacing dynamic clipping threshold with Clip-Higher and Clip-Lower can be found in the cite38†Appendix E .
